## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Acris, Ganimian, King, and Marple-Cantrell report a clean school-randomized trial of a USAID-funded civics program in 140 Liberian public primary schools (70 treatment, 70 control, stratified by county and district) and find that after one school year grade 3–4 students in treatment schools scored 0.379 SD (SE 0.086) higher on a civic knowledge assessment (Table 3, Panel A), with the gain concentrated in the "knowing" cognitive domain (0.370) and in the society-and-systems (0.284) and participation (0.364) content domains, and no detectable effect on reasoning-and-applying (0.076, SE 0.085), civic principles, civic identities, or three self-reported civic behaviors (index 0.003, SE 0.015; Table 6). The core estimate is credibly identified: baseline balance is good (joint F p = .444), attrition is 15% and non-differential (−0.006, SE 0.020), contamination is measured rather than assumed (6 of 70 control principals reported teaching civics), and the effect sits far from any significance threshold. The field can cite this as the first school-based experimental evidence on children's civic knowledge in a low-income, post-conflict setting, and as good feasibility evidence that individual take-home textbooks and a timetabled twice-weekly subject can be delivered with high fidelity in such a system. What needs qualification is almost everything built on top of that number. The assessment was written to the treatment curriculum and given to control students who mostly received no civics instruction at all, so 0.38 SD is the effect of teaching a subject on a test of that subject; the comparisons to LMIC math-and-reading meta-analyses ("more than double") and the conversion to "38 ICCS points" (p. 11) rest on an unstated and unsupported equivalence of standard deviations and should not travel. The intervention is a four-part bundle (textbooks, 2-day training, twice-weekly lessons, twice-monthly monitoring), so the paper's third claimed contribution — a lesson for the textbook-provision literature — and the abstract's "textbook-centered instruction" mechanism cannot be separated from added instructional time, and the classroom observations (60 schools, one lesson each, with the comparison lesson in control schools unspecified) describe what treatment classrooms did, not what caused the gains. The engagement null covers three dichotomized prosocial self-reports with control means of 0.75–0.84, while attitude outcomes — a primary outcome in the study's AEA registry entry — are reported only "upon request." The one significant heterogeneity result is understated: Table 4, column 5 implies an effect of −0.18 SD (n.s.) in non-rural districts and about +0.53 SD in rural ones, which the Discussion softens to "somewhat larger" and the Conclusion to "across a broad range of students," though the specification swaps strata for county fixed effects and the number of districts is never reported. Finally, the pre-analysis plan was first published June 24, 2024 — the intervention's listed end date and roughly nine months after baseline — and the PDF carries no data, code, or software statement, so the subscale, heterogeneity, and mechanism results should be read as exploratory and nothing beyond the arithmetic of the printed tables can be independently verified. The right posture: rely on the headline knowledge effect and the knowing-versus-reasoning profile as printed in Table 3; attach caveats to the magnitude benchmarks, the textbook mechanism, the breadth of the engagement null, and the generality of the effect across urban and rural districts; and treat "a scalable model for strengthening democratic foundations in fragile states" as aspiration rather than finding.

#### Key Strengths

- Design and execution are sound and well documented: school-level randomization matching school-wide delivery, stratification by county and district, 140 clusters, good balance on 13 baseline characteristics (Table 1, joint F = 1.011, p = .444), 85% follow-up with a −0.6 percentage-point differential and a null joint attrition test (Table 2, p = .323), measured contamination (6 of 70 control principals teaching civics, 8 of 70 with textbooks, 3 with both), and reported implementation fidelity (textbooks in 100% of treatment schools, 96% of students confirming receipt, 94% training participation, 38-minute observed lessons).
- The headline effect is large and precisely estimated (0.379 SD, SE 0.086, t ≈ 4.4; Table 3), the quantile and baseline-percentile analyses show positive point estimates throughout the distribution (Figure 1), and there is no detectable heterogeneity by gender, grade, household assets, or home language (Table 4, columns 1–4). As evidence that Liberian children learn curricular civics content when it is actually delivered, the result is solid.
- The paper reports its nulls candidly and in the tables: reasoning-and-applying, civic principles, civic identities, and all three engagement items are shown with standard errors; the abstract states the engagement null; ceiling effects on engagement and the fixed-effects substitution behind the rural estimate are flagged by the authors themselves.
- The setting is genuinely under-studied — primary-grade, school-based civics in a low-income, post-conflict African country — and the Discussion's generalizability paragraph (p. 17) is more explicit than most, naming the three features of Liberia that bound the result and candidate replication settings.
- The headline specification (Equation 1: ANCOVA with baseline score, strata fixed effects, school-clustered SEs) is stated plainly, and the reported numbers reconcile: sample flow (167 − 22 = 145 eligible; 44 + 48 + 48 = 140), Ns (1,101 + 1,006 = 2,107; 936 + 848 = 1,784), follow-up rates (936/1,101 = 0.850), Table 5 row sums, the 15-percentile and 8-percentage-point derivations, and significance stars against coefficient/SE ratios all check.

#### Key Concerns

- The estimand is narrower than the framing. Control schools mostly taught no civics (pp. 5–6) and the test was "aligned with the Grade 3 and Grade 4 Liberian civic education curriculum" that only treatment schools received (p. 8), so 0.38 SD measures instruction in a body of content against a no-instruction counterfactual on a test of that content. The benchmarks on p. 11 — "more than double" the 0.08–0.15 SD LMIC meta-analytic range and "roughly equivalent to a 38-point increase on the ICCS scale," moving "from Colombia (482) to just above the international average (517)" — treat it as a general achievement gain. The meta-analysis comparison carries a subject-matter caveat but not an alignment caveat; the ICCS conversion carries no caveat at all and assumes one SD among Liberian third and fourth graders equals 100 ICCS points among eighth graders in 24 countries. The literature reviewer also notes the "467 to 586" range omits at least two lower-scoring ICCS 2016 participants (Peru, Dominican Republic).
- The mechanism and textbook claims outrun the design. Textbooks came bundled with a new timetabled subject, teacher training, and twice-monthly NGO monitoring (pp. 6–7), so nothing separates materials from instructional time; the contrast with textbook-provision nulls (Glewwe et al., 2009; Sabarwal et al., 2014), where books were added to subjects already taught, is not like-for-like. The classroom-observation evidence (Table 5) is descriptive, from one observed lesson in each of 60 schools, with observers necessarily unblinded, the comparison lesson in control schools unspecified, and no measure of "rote memorization" despite the p. 3 claim; the Teach Primary pedagogy tool was dropped for reliability (fn. 4). The student textbook-use figures (63% vs. 2%, p. 12) appear in no exhibit in the main paper.
- The engagement null is thinner than "no impact on students' civic engagement" (abstract) suggests, and the null subscales are imprecise. Engagement is three self-reported prosocial items dichotomized from a 4-point scale with control means of 0.751–0.843 (Table 6); attitudes, which the registry lists as a primary outcome, are "available upon request" (fn. 3); and the civic identities domain — the content closest to the paper's post-conflict rationale — shows 0.021 (SE 0.067) without discussion. Realized power is below plan (footnote 1's MDE of 0.17 SD assumed a 0.40 baseline–endline correlation and 15 students per cluster; the realized SE of 0.086 implies an MDE near 0.24 SD, the baseline slope is 0.226, and the endline cluster size is about 12.7), so the "null" subscales cannot rule out effects of roughly +0.15 to +0.27 SD, and the knowing-versus-reasoning contrast is never formally tested.
- The rural heterogeneity result is understated and fragile at once. Table 4, column 5 gives a treatment coefficient of −0.177 (SE 0.219) for non-rural districts and an interaction of 0.706 (SE 0.238), implying roughly zero effect in urban districts and about 0.53 SD in rural ones; the Results call this "substantially stronger gains in rural schools relative to urban schools" (p. 12), the Discussion "somewhat larger improvements" that were "broadly shared" (p. 16), and the Conclusion gains "across a broad range of students" (p. 17), and neither the abstract nor the generalizability paragraph mentions it. At the same time the specification drops the strata fixed effects for county fixed effects (the paper's stated reason — that because rurality is district-level the strata fixed effects "cannot be included" — is not right, since only the rural main effect is absorbed and the interaction remains identified), "rural district" is undefined, and the number of districts behind the moderator is unreported.
- Pre-registration, reproducibility, and several prose–exhibit lapses limit what can be verified. The pre-analysis plan was "first published on June 24, 2024" (fn. 5), the intervention's registry end date and about nine months after baseline, and the paper neither says so nor reports which outcomes were pre-specified; the PDF has no data availability, code, or software statement; the outcome metric is described as standardized "at baseline" (p. 10) but "in the control group" in the Table 3 note (endline control mean exactly 0.000 [1.000]); "all analyses control for students' baseline assessment scores" (p. 10) does not match the Table 5 or Table 6 notes; the attrition sentence (p. 8) reports the age × treatment interaction (−0.015, significant only at 10%) as the treatment-group age gradient and calls it "statistically significant"; and fidelity statistics shift between sections ("100% of teachers," p. 2, vs. "100% of treatment schools," p. 7; "96% … confirming receipt," p. 7, vs. "96% … receiving and regularly using," p. 17) with no exhibit for any of them.

#### What to Rely On

- After one school year, the program raised scores on a curriculum-aligned civic knowledge assessment by 0.379 SD (SE 0.086; 95% CI ≈ 0.21–0.55; Table 3, Panel A). This is the load-bearing, well-identified result; quote it as the effect of introducing a structured civics course, in the paper's endline-control-SD units.
- The profile of the gain: large on the "knowing" domain (0.370, SE 0.078) and on society-and-systems (0.284) and participation (0.364) content, small and insignificant on reasoning-and-applying (0.076), principles (0.091), and identities (0.021) (Table 3, Panels B–C) — as a description of point estimates, not as a tested contrast.
- Point-estimate gains at every percentile of the endline distribution and at every baseline-score percentile (Figure 1), with somewhat larger gains in the middle, and no detectable heterogeneity by gender, grade, household assets, or home language (Table 4, columns 1–4).
- Feasibility and fidelity: textbooks and a timetabled twice-weekly subject were delivered at scale in a low-resource system; treatment teachers taught with a textbook 57% of class time versus 15% in control and used the blackboard 25% versus 50% (Table 5, Panel B); time on learning activities was unchanged at about 77% (Panel A); whole-class engagement rose from 71% to 87% of class time (Panel C).
- A precisely estimated one-year null on three self-reported everyday behaviors — helping classmates, helping neighbors, obeying community laws — with the index CI about −0.03 to +0.03 and no item upper bound above roughly 8 percentage points (Table 6). Describe these as prosocial self-reports near ceiling, not civic or political engagement generally.
- Low, balanced attrition (85% follow-up; treatment differential −0.006, SE 0.020; joint interaction test p = .323; Table 2) and good baseline balance (Table 1).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "More than double" the LMIC meta-analytic average and "a 38-point increase on the ICCS scale" (p. 11) — the test was aligned to a curriculum the control group did not receive, the SD-equivalence with the ICCS scale is assumed rather than shown, and the quoted ICCS floor of 467 omits lower-scoring participants; do not carry these into citations or briefs.
- "Knowledge gains were driven by textbook-centered instruction rather than shifts in pedagogy" (pp. 2–3) and the contribution to the textbook-provision literature (pp. 3, 16–17) — a four-component bundle cannot isolate textbooks; the observation data are descriptive, unblinded, and lack a specified comparison lesson; and the 63% vs. 2% student textbook-use figures have no exhibit.
- "The program had no impact on students' civic engagement" (abstract) — three dichotomized self-report items with control means of 0.75–0.84; attitudes (a registered primary outcome) are unreported; read as "no detectable change in three everyday prosocial self-reports within one year."
- "Positive effects across the achievement distribution" (abstract), "broadly shared" (p. 16), and "across a diverse student body" (p. 17) — the Figure 1 confidence bands include zero at roughly the top fifth of the endline distribution, and the point estimates in Table 4, column 5 imply no gain in urban districts.
- The rural interaction itself (0.706, Table 4, column 5) — estimated with county rather than strata fixed effects, on an undefined "rural district" indicator with an unreported number of districts; do not cite the rural concentration as established, but do not cite the pooled effect as uniform across settings either.
- "Gains concentrated in factual knowledge" as a contrast — the subscale CIs reach about +0.24 SD (reasoning) and +0.27 SD (principles), the percent-correct subscales have unreported item counts and reliability, and the difference between domains is never tested.
- "The first experimental evidence on the effectiveness of civic education in a low-income, post-conflict setting" (Conclusion, p. 17) — defensible only with the introduction's qualifiers ("school-based," "student civic outcomes"); the literature reviewer identifies randomized adult civic-education trials in Liberia (Mvukiyehe & Samii, 2017) and Mali (Gottlieb, 2016) that are not cited.
- Several characterizations of prior work — Green et al. (2011), Morduchowicz et al. (1996), and NORC (2019) as high-income-country studies (p. 16; Argentina and Georgia are middle-income); Morduchowicz et al. as a secondary-level evaluation (p. 3); Nie & Hillygus (2001) and Niemi & Junn (1998) as longitudinal evidence on childhood civic knowledge (p. 3); Alan et al. (2021) and Dhar et al. (2022) as examples of complements "harder to implement in low-resource settings" (p. 16) when both changed behavior through school-delivered curricula in middle-income public schools. Verify before repeating.
- Any number quoted from the prose without an exhibit — student textbook use (63%/2%), every fidelity statistic (100%, 96%, 94%, 94%, 38 minutes, 29 of 48), "baseline levels of reported civic engagement were already high" (p. 16; Table 6 shows only endline means), and the attrition gradient ("1.5 percentage points for each year of age," p. 8, which is the interaction coefficient, significant at 10%, not the within-treatment gradient of about 2.3 points).
- "A scalable model for strengthening democratic foundations in fragile states" (p. 17) — no cost data are reported, delivery ran through donor-funded NGOs with twice-monthly monitoring the authors concede may be hard to sustain, and none of the outcomes tied to democratic foundations (identities, attitudes, behaviors) moved.
- The study's status as pre-registered and its verifiability — registration was first published June 24, 2024, after baseline and at the listed end of the intervention; no PAP-deviation discussion, data, code, or software statement exists in the PDF; the outcome standardization is described two different ways; and thirteen supplementary items (Figures A.1–A.2, Table A.1, Appendices B.1–B.5) that carry instrument details, item counts, and the theory of change do not travel with the article.

#### Verification notes

- Headline and subscale effects (abstract, pp. 2, 11 vs. Table 3): 0.38/0.379***, 0.37/0.370***, 0.36/0.364***, 0.28/0.284***; nulls 0.091, 0.021, 0.076 unstarred — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 11).
- Rural specification (Table 4, column 5): treatment −0.177 (0.219), covariate −0.335 (0.214), interaction 0.706*** (0.238); implied rural effect ≈ 0.53, urban ≈ −0.18 — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 14).
- Student textbook use "63% vs. 2%" (p. 12) has no row in Table 5, whose Panel B is labeled "(teachers)" — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 15).
- Attrition sentence (p. 8) vs. Table 2, Panel B: Age −0.008 (0.006), Age × Treatment −0.015* (0.008); the 1.5-point figure is the interaction and is significant at 10% only — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 9).
- Standardization: "at baseline" (p. 10) vs. "in the control group" (Table 3 note) with endline control at 0.000 [1.000] and baseline treatment at 0.043 [1.075] (Table 1) — CONFIRMED.
- Figure 1: the lower 95% band crosses zero at roughly the top fifth of the endline distribution (Panel A) and near the top of the baseline distribution (Panel B) — CONFIRMED (rendered p. 13).
- Table 5 row sums to 1.00 within each panel; significance stars consistent with coefficient/SE ratios in Tables 2–6 — CONFIRMED.
- Fidelity text shifts ("100% of teachers," p. 2 vs. "100% of treatment schools," p. 7; "confirming receipt," p. 7 vs. "receiving and regularly using," p. 17) — CONFIRMED from the text.
- Power arithmetic: 2.8 × 0.086 ≈ 0.24 SD realized MDE vs. 0.17 planned (fn. 1); baseline slope 0.226 (Table 4, column 6); endline cluster size 1,784/140 ≈ 12.7 — CONFIRMED.
- Implied grade effects from Table 4, column 1 (0.431 grade 3; 0.431 − 0.105 = 0.326 grade 4) — CONFIRMED.
- Conclusion (p. 17) drops the introduction's "student civic outcomes" qualifier from the first-evidence claim — CONFIRMED.
- AEA RCT Registry AEARCTR-0013817 (fetched independently): initial registration June 14, 2024; first published June 24, 2024; intervention September 25, 2023 to June 24, 2024; primary outcomes "student civic knowledge, student civic attitudes, student civic behaviors"; no public PAP document — CONFIRMED.
- Reproducibility review's registry discrepancy on stratification ("by county" vs. the paper's county and district) — CORRECTED: the registry line describes the 44/48/48 sample allocation across counties, not necessarily the randomization strata; not a clear discrepancy.
- Reproducibility review's statement that the registry lists grades 3–4 (vs. the paper's grades 1–6) as receiving the intervention — COULD NOT CHECK (not returned by the overseer's fetch).
- Literature review's external claims (Mvukiyehe & Samii 2017 and Gottlieb 2016 as uncited adult civic-education RCTs; ICCS 2016 scores for Peru and the Dominican Republic below 467; Morduchowicz et al. 1996 as a grade 5–6 program; McEwan 2015 category means) — COULD NOT CHECK against the paper; consistent with the overseer's own knowledge but not independently verified here.
- Absence of any data availability, code, or software statement in the PDF — CONFIRMED by text search ("upon request" appears only in footnotes 3–4; "replication" only in the Discussion's replication-studies sentence).

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This school-randomized evaluation provides credible evidence that a supported civic education package in Liberian public primary schools improved curriculum-aligned civic knowledge among pupils observed at follow-up. The reported adjusted effect is 0.379 SD (SE 0.086; p. 11, Table 3). The intervention combined textbooks, teacher training, scheduled instruction, and monitoring, so its success belongs to that package (pp. 6–7). It produced no statistically detectable change in the measured self-reported everyday civic behaviors (p. 15, Table 6). My judgment is that this is useful evidence for the feasibility of civic knowledge instruction in a resource-constrained setting, but readers should qualify claims about general civic competence, universal benefit, pedagogical mechanisms, and democratic consequences. Incomplete follow-up and an unresolved score-normalization ambiguity limit interpretation, while missing replication materials limit independent verification. The strong contribution rating and weak reproducibility rating address different questions: the experiment adds meaningful evidence, but the published documentation does not enable its full reconstruction. Neither the documentation gaps nor the secondary-analysis concerns demonstrate that the main knowledge estimate is wrong.

#### Key Strengths

- The main causal comparison is well founded: schools were randomly assigned within geographic strata, and the principal analysis retains strata controls, baseline adjustment, and school-clustered standard errors (pp. 5–6, 10; p. 11, Table 3). My judgment is that this supports substantial weight on the average knowledge finding, subject to outcome availability.
- The knowledge gain is clearly distinguishable from zero in the reported analysis: 0.379 SD (SE 0.086), with a knowing-domain estimate of 0.370 SD (SE 0.078; p. 11, Table 3). These document learning on the adapted assessment rather than merely improved attitudes toward the program.
- The paper makes an important contextual contribution by testing supported civic instruction in Liberian primary schools and connecting civic-learning research with evidence on instructional materials (pp. 2–3, 6–7, 16–17). Its importance lies in the setting and tested delivery model; an exhaustive claim of priority is unnecessary.
- Classroom observations add evidence about implementation: the adjusted increase in teacher textbook use is 0.402 of class time (SE 0.080; p. 15, Table 5). These observations help characterize the program without identifying which component caused learning.
- The article is navigable, separates knowledge from reported behavior, and reports group means, adjusted contrasts, uncertainty, and follow-up diagnostics (pp. 9–15, Tables 2–6). This makes its central findings more auditable than its broad summary language sometimes suggests.

#### Key Concerns

- Missing outcomes remain a causal limitation: the baseline sample contains 2,107 pupils (p. 6, Table 1), while the assessment analysis contains 1,784 (p. 11, Table 3). The adjusted follow-up difference is −0.006 (SE 0.020), with a joint interaction-test p-value of .323 (p. 9, Table 2). These are reassuring diagnostics, not proof that unobserved outcomes are ignorable; no attrition sensitivity analysis is supplied.
- The reported effect-size denominator is ambiguous: p. 10 says scores are standardized to have “mean zero and SD one at baseline,” whereas the Table 3 note says “mean zero and SD one in the control group” (p. 11). Successive rescaling could reconcile these statements, but is not explained. The supplied article also lacks a documented data-access route, replication code, and sufficient scoring details to reconstruct the knowledge outcome. Online supplements are not bound into the PDF and were unavailable; their contents cannot be assumed deficient.
- Broader outcome and mechanism claims exceed the identified contrast. Engagement covers self-reported helping and law obedience, with responses dichotomized before averaging (p. 15, Table 6); classroom material use is a post-treatment outcome (p. 15, Table 5). My judgment is that neither general behavioral ineffectiveness nor textbook mediation follows from these measures and comparisons.
- Secondary findings deserve less weight than the main mean contrast: upper-tail uncertainty reaches zero in Figure 1 (p. 13), the rural interaction uses county rather than randomization-strata fixed effects (p. 14, Table 4), and the article reports no direct cognitive-domain contrast or multiplicity adjustment (pp. 10–14). These limitations weaken universal-benefit and targeting claims without invalidating the main randomized comparison.
- Policy and literature framing require restraint. Eligibility excludes less accessible schools, and delivery includes external implementation support (pp. 5–8); persistence, routine-delivery costs, and democratic effects are not established (pp. 16–17). The broad claim to first experimental evidence also overlooks earlier community civic education in Liberia; the school-based contribution remains valuable. See the original [Community Empowerment Program report, executive summary](https://poverty-action.org/sites/default/files/publications/blattman_hartman_blair_can_we_teach_peace_ipa_liberia_0.pdf).

#### What to Rely On

- Offering the complete supported program improved the locally adapted civic-knowledge assessment in the reassessed sample: the adjusted overall contrast is 0.379 SD (SE 0.086; p. 11, Table 3), with causal interpretation conditional on the missing-outcome limitation and magnitude subject to the normalization ambiguity.
- The program yielded no statistically detectable short-run change in the particular self-reported behaviors measured: the engagement-index contrast is 0.003 (SE 0.015; p. 15, Table 6). This is a finding about that instrument and follow-up period.
- Observed classrooms used textbooks more and showed greater whole-class engagement under the program (p. 15, Table 5); these are useful implementation findings, not an identified pathway from textbook use to achievement.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Claims that civic knowledge cannot change civic behavior or strengthen democracy: the measured everyday behaviors do not establish effects on political participation, democratic tolerance, reconciliation, or later outcomes (p. 15, Table 6; pp. 16–18). The broader literature is not uniformly null either: [USAID’s account of the Georgia evaluation](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USAIDHQ/bulletins/336cde0) reports positive participation and discussion findings; this check concerns the sponsor’s summary, not the full evaluation.
- Claims that higher-order learning was absent or that the cognitive-domain effects differ: reasoning and applying has an estimate of 0.076 SD (SE 0.085), and Table 3 provides no direct between-domain test (p. 11). Statistical inconclusiveness is not a demonstrated zero or a significant difference between effects.
- Claims that all students benefited or that rural targeting is established: Figure 1’s marginal distributions do not identify individual effects and its upper-tail bands include zero (p. 13); the rural interaction of 0.706 (SE 0.238) uses a changed specification (p. 14, Table 4). My methodological judgment is that district-level rural status does not itself require dropping strata controls to estimate the treatment-by-rural interaction.
- Claims that textbooks alone caused the gain, didactic teaching outperforms participatory teaching, or the program will scale cheaply: the trial compares the entire supported package with the control condition, without isolating components or testing alternative pedagogies, long-run sustainability, or cost-effectiveness (pp. 6–7, 16–17; p. 15, Table 5).
- Claims of equivalence to international civic-assessment performance or an unqualified first experiment in post-conflict civic education: the local assessment is adapted rather than demonstrably equated to ICCS (pp. 8–11; p. 11, Table 3), and the earlier [Liberian community experiment](https://poverty-action.org/sites/default/files/publications/blattman_hartman_blair_can_we_teach_peace_ipa_liberia_0.pdf) limits broad novelty claims without negating the school-based contribution.

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: the overall effect is 0.379 (SE 0.086), knowing is 0.370 (0.078), and reasoning/applying is 0.076 (0.085), exactly as reported in p. 11, Table 3.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/reproducibility: baseline N = 2,107 (p. 6, Table 1), endline N = 1,784 (p. 11, Table 3), and the adjusted follow-up contrast is −0.006 (0.020), with joint p = .323 (p. 9, Table 2).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing/reproducibility: the baseline-versus-control normalization descriptions differ as quoted above; the paper does not explain a rescaling sequence (p. 10; p. 11, Table 3).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: p. 8 describes reassessment as “decreasing by about 1.5 percentage points for each year of age,” but Table 2 reports “Age −0.008 (0.006)” and “Age × Treatment −0.015* (0.008)” (p. 9); my sum is −0.023 for the treatment-group age slope, confirming the review’s correction of the paper’s interpretation.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing: visual inspection of p. 13, Figure 1 confirms upper-tail bands include zero; p. 12’s “students at every level of prior achievement benefited” is stronger than its own qualification that gains “become statistically insignificant at the top of the distribution.”
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: teacher textbook use rises by 0.402 (0.080), and the engagement-index contrast is 0.003 (0.015), as verified visually in p. 15, Tables 5 and 6; the latter note confirms dichotomized self-reports.
- CONFIRMED — Methods: the rural interaction is 0.706 (0.238), and its regression substitutes county for strata fixed effects (p. 14, Table 4); the review’s objection to the necessity of that substitution is a methodological judgment.
- CONFIRMED — Literature: the earlier [Community Empowerment Program report](https://poverty-action.org/sites/default/files/publications/blattman_hartman_blair_can_we_teach_peace_ipa_liberia_0.pdf) documents a randomized Liberian community civic-education intervention; [USAID’s Georgia summary](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USAIDHQ/bulletins/336cde0) reports positive school-political participation and discussion outcomes, supporting the review’s limited citation checks.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Writing flags prose-only student textbook-use percentages on p. 12; Table 5’s materials panel is labeled “(teachers)” (p. 15), so no displayed student-use row verifies those percentages; they are not used here.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reproducibility: full scoring reconstruction, unavailable supplemental instruments, and adherence to the registered plan cannot be verified from the bound article; p. 18 identifies online supplements and on-request results but does not supply them.

#### Per-Dimension Ratings

| Dimension | Rating | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Methods | adequate | high (0.90) |
| Literature | adequate | high (0.87) |
| Writing | adequate | high (0.94) |
| Contribution | strong | high (0.90) |
| Reproducibility | weak | high (0.94) |

:::
